outcome: Since 26 January 2024 the planar conjecture (a strictly convex integrable billiard table has an elliptical boundary) has not been settled. The in-window papers are local, analogue, special-case or namesake results, and the latest status statements (Bialy and Mironov's October 2025 survey, Glutsyuk's September 2025 paper, and Koval's May 2026 talk) still describe the general problem as open.
problem_asks: The Wikipedia bullet: 'if a billiard table is strictly convex and integrable, is its boundary necessarily an ellipse?' Unpacked: (1) Objects: planar billiard tables whose boundary is a strictly convex closed curve. The bullet does not say whether tables are bounded, nor what smoothness the boundary has; the literature works with smooth boundaries (C-infinity or analytic), and several results need only C2 or C1. (2) Hypothesis: the billiard is 'integrable'. The bullet does not fix the notion. The literature uses several: caustic-integrable (a neighbourhood of the boundary foliated by caustics or invariant curves); total integrability (the phase cylinder foliated by non-contractible invariant curves); a first integral with nonvanishing gradient; polynomial integrability (a non-constant first integral polynomial in the velocity); integrability only near the boundary; integrability only away from the boundary. (3) Conclusion: the boundary is an ellipse, with the circle as a special case. The bullet asks only the forward implication. The converse (ellipses are integrable, a classical fact) is not asked. No bound, effective version, higher-dimensional version or other billiard model is asked. To track: (a) the general planar claim for all smooth strictly convex integrable tables under each variant of the hypothesis; (b) the local claim near ellipses, which is a restricted case, not the whole.

events.what_happened: H. Poritsky, 'The billiard ball problem on a table with a convex boundary: an illustrative dynamical problem', Annals of Mathematics (1950). Secondary sources say this is where the conjecture first appears in print, attributed to Birkhoff, and that Poritsky proved it under an extra nested-caustic assumption. I did not open the paper.
events.delivers: Per secondary reports only: the boundary is an ellipse under an extra assumption (for nested closed caustics near the boundary, the smaller is a caustic of the billiard in the bigger one). The exact hypothesis is unverified.
events.remains: Everything outside that nested-caustic assumption.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record in which the paper was published
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper; the refereeing is not visible to me

events.doubts: Only secondary descriptions read; the Annals paper itself was not opened.
events.direction: Partial positive result for the conjecture, under an extra hypothesis.
people: G. D. Birkhoff (credited with the conjecture)

events.what_happened: M. Bialy's theorem on totally integrable billiards: if the phase cylinder is foliated by continuous closed invariant curves that are not null-homotopic, the table is a disc. The journal is Mathematische Zeitschrift, 1993 per the search digest, though one secondary source (Baracco and Bernardi, 2023) says 1992. I did not open the paper; I know it from secondary summaries.
events.delivers: The circle only, and only under global total integrability (the whole phase cylinder foliated by non-contractible invariant curves).
events.remains: Every non-circular ellipse; any weaker form of integrability (caustics near the boundary only, or first integrals without a global foliation).
events.doubts: Year disputed (1992 vs 1993) between secondary sources. Paper not read.
events.direction: Circle special case under a global hypothesis; positive for the conjecture in that case.

events.what_happened: V. Kaloshin and A. Sorrentino, 'On conjugacy of convex billiards', arXiv:1203.1274 (submitted 6 March 2012). The abstract says they resolve a question of Guillemin (C^{1,alpha}-conjugacy of billiard maps near the boundary, alpha > 1/2, forces the domains to be similar), use this to prove a conditional version of Birkhoff's conjecture, and show the original conjecture is equivalent to what they call an 'Extension problem'.
events.delivers: A conditional version of the conjecture, conditional on a hypothesis that I did not extract, plus a reformulation of the full conjecture as an equivalent extension problem.
events.remains: The conjecture itself, unconditionally.
events.doubts: The conditional hypothesis is not recorded because I read only the abstract page.
events.direction: Reformulation plus conditional partial result; no unconditional claim.

events.what_happened: A. Avila, J. De Simoi and V. Kaloshin, 'An integrable deformation of an ellipse of small eccentricity is an ellipse', arXiv:1412.2853 (v1 9 December 2014; v4 9 February 2016), Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016) 527-558.
events.revisions: v2 3 Sep 2015; v3 9 Dec 2015; v4 9 Feb 2016; published Annals 184(2), 2016.
events.delivers: Small perturbations of an ellipse of small eccentricity that remain integrable are ellipses. This is a restricted local version: small eccentricity and small perturbation.
events.remains: Ellipses of eccentricity that is not small; large perturbations; the general case.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published after refereeing (referee process not visible to me)

events.direction: Positive for the conjecture in a restricted local class.

events.what_happened: V. Kaloshin and A. Sorrentino, 'On the local Birkhoff conjecture for convex billiards', arXiv:1612.09194 (v1 29 December 2016; v5 21 March 2018), Annals of Mathematics 188 (2018) 315-380. The paper proves a complete local version: a small integrable deformation of an ellipse is an ellipse. Its introduction, which I read, proposes an affine length-shortening (ALS) flow strategy toward the global case, described as an outline in Appendix F.
events.revisions: v2 18 Jan 2017; v3 29 Mar 2017; v4 28 Jul 2017; v5 21 Mar 2018 (current, Annals version).
events.delivers: A small integrable deformation of an ellipse that is strictly convex and remains integrable is an ellipse. Local: 'small' is the only restriction stated in the paraphrase I read; no eccentricity restriction appears in my paraphrase.
events.remains: Large deformations and the global conjecture. Appendix F outlines an ALS strategy toward the global case; the introduction calls this a strategy, and the paper does not claim the global case.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published after refereeing (referee process not visible to me)

events.doubts: Appendix F was not read directly (the PDF text was not extractable); its content is taken from the introduction's description.
events.direction: Positive for the conjecture in the local class; the global outline is a plan only.

events.what_happened: G. Huang, V. Kaloshin and A. Sorrentino, 'Nearly circular domains which are integrable close to the boundary are ellipses', arXiv:1705.10601 (v1 28 May 2017; v3 16 Feb 2018), Geometric and Functional Analysis 28(2) (2018) 334-392.
events.revisions: v2 27 Dec 2017; v3 16 Feb 2018 (final, to appear in GAFA).
events.delivers: A domain that is a small perturbation of an ellipse of small eccentricity and remains integrable near its boundary is an ellipse. The paper also notes that local integrability near the boundary forces global integrability. Hypothesis is weaker than full integrability, so it is a changed version of the question.
events.remains: Large eccentricity and large perturbations; the global conjecture as posed (with integrability assumed everywhere).

checked_by.what_they_did: Published after refereeing (referee process not visible to me)

events.direction: Positive for the conjecture in a restricted local class, under integrability near the boundary.

events.what_happened: A. Glutsyuk, 'On polynomially integrable Birkhoff billiards on surfaces of constant curvature', arXiv:1706.04030 (v1 13 June 2017; v7 22 Feb 2019), Journal of the European Mathematical Society 23(3) (2021) 995-1049, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1027. Builds on Bialy and Mironov's reduction (2016-2017) to an algebro-geometric problem, which Glutsyuk solves.
events.revisions: v2 31 Jul 2017; v3 5 Jan 2018; v4 8 Feb 2018; v5 21 Jul 2018; v6 17 Jan 2019; v7 22 Feb 2019; published JEMS 2021.
events.delivers: A bounded convex planar billiard with a smooth boundary that is polynomially integrable (admits a non-constant first integral polynomial in the velocity) is an ellipse. The paper also covers non-convex piecewise-smooth boundaries on the plane, sphere and hyperbolic plane. This is a different-hypotheses version: integrability is restricted to polynomial first integrals, so it settles the algebraic version only.
events.remains: Integrability by non-polynomial first integrals or by caustics, which is the question as posed.

checked_by.who: Journal of the European Mathematical Society
checked_by.what_they_did: Published after refereeing (referee process not visible to me)

checked_by.who: M. Bialy and A. Mironov, in their 2025 survey
checked_by.qualification: Experts on the problem, co-authors of the two papers that the algebraic proof rests on
checked_by.what_they_did: Describe the algebraic version as proved by Glutsyuk, with the restriction to polynomial integrals

events.doubts: Scope wording is disputed between sources: the search digest says the theorem requires a connected C2 boundary, but the arXiv abstract I read says 'smooth'. The JEMS version was not read.
events.direction: Positive for the algebraic version; a restricted case of the problem.

events.what_happened: G. Huang and V. Kaloshin, 'On the finite dimensionality of integrable deformations of strictly convex integrable billiard tables', arXiv:1809.09341 (v1 25 September 2018; v2 26 October 2018).
events.revisions: v2 26 Oct 2018; no journal publication found.
events.delivers: Smooth one-parameter families of tables that start at a strictly convex table integrable near the boundary and stay integrable near the boundary: their initial velocity lies in a finite-dimensional linear space through the original table. A structural rigidity statement; it does not conclude that the boundary is an ellipse.
events.remains: The conjecture itself.
events.direction: Structural result near the conjectured class; no verdict on the conclusion.

events.what_happened: M. Bialy and A. E. Mironov, 'The Birkhoff-Poritsky conjecture for centrally-symmetric billiard tables', arXiv:2008.03566 (v1 8 August 2020; v4 28 February 2022), Annals of Mathematics 196(1) (2022) 389-413. Proves the conjecture for centrally symmetric C2 convex planar tables under any of three hypotheses: C0 invariant curves foliating the region between the invariant curve of 4-periodic orbits and the boundary; a C1 foliation by convex caustics with rotation numbers in (0, 1/4] near the boundary (the original Birkhoff-Poritsky form); or a C1 first integral with nonvanishing gradient.
events.revisions: v2 13 Aug 2020; v3 13 Dec 2020; v4 28 Feb 2022 (Annals version).
events.delivers: For centrally symmetric C2 convex planar tables, the boundary is an ellipse under each of the three hypotheses listed above. A restricted class (centrally symmetric) plus foliation-type hypotheses.
events.remains: Tables that are not centrally symmetric, and the general case without a foliation hypothesis.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published after refereeing (referee process not visible to me)

checked_by.who: V. Kaloshin, C. E. Koudjinan and K. Zhang
checked_by.qualification: Experts in billiard dynamics; authors of the perturbative extension
checked_by.what_they_did: Build on the Bialy-Mironov result to prove a perturbative version

events.direction: Positive for the conjecture in a restricted class (centrally symmetric), under foliation or first-integral hypotheses.

events.what_happened: I. Koval, 'Local strong Birkhoff conjecture and local spectral rigidity of almost every ellipse', arXiv:2111.12171 (v1 23 November 2021; v2 15 February 2023). Proves that a small perturbation of almost every ellipse that preserves integrability near the boundary is itself an ellipse; applies this to spectral rigidity. The same result is the subject of a talk at Beijing Normal University on 12 May 2026 (see sources); the talk is not a new event.
events.revisions: v2 15 Feb 2023. No journal publication found in my searches.
events.delivers: For almost every ellipse (eccentricities in a full-measure set), a small perturbation that keeps integrability near the boundary is an ellipse. Restricted to a full-measure set of ellipses, local, and under the near-boundary integrability hypothesis.
events.remains: The ellipses in the complementary null set; global integrability.
events.doubts: Only the arXiv abstract was read; the full text and any referee report were not seen. No journal publication found, so it is not established that the result has been refereed.
events.direction: Positive for the conjecture in a restricted local class.

events.what_happened: G. Huang, 'On the integrability of strictly convex billiard tables with boundaries close to ellipses with small eccentricities', Acta Mathematica Sinica, English Series 38(1) (2022) 55-67, DOI 10.1007/s10114-022-0153-3. Introduces 'integrability away from the boundary', in which the integrable region can sit at a positive distance from the boundary. No arXiv preprint was found, so the journal month is the earliest date I can give.
events.delivers: For a strictly convex table whose boundary is a small perturbation of an ellipse with small eccentricity, integrability away from the boundary forces the boundary to be an ellipse. Restricted (small eccentricity, small perturbation) and under a changed hypothesis (integrability away from the boundary).
events.remains: Large eccentricity and large perturbations; the general case.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published after refereeing (referee process not visible to me)

events.doubts: The Springer full text redirected and was not opened. Abstract read via a university repository record.
events.direction: Positive for the conjecture in a restricted local class under a changed hypothesis.

events.what_happened: Q. Wang and K. Zhang, 'Gevrey regularity for the formally linearizable billiard of Treschev', arXiv:2211.03182 (6 November 2022). Treschev gave formal power series for a billiard whose dynamics are locally linearizable near a periodic orbit. Wang and Zhang show that, when the linear frequency is Diophantine, the series is Gevrey regular of order 1+alpha for some alpha > 0. They do not establish analyticity or convergence.
events.delivers: Gevrey regularity of a formal, locally linearizable billiard for Diophantine frequency. It is a formal object near a periodic orbit, not a global table, and says nothing about the conjecture unless the series converges.
events.remains: Convergence (analyticity) of the Treschev example; the conjecture itself. A secondary report says that convergence would give a local counterexample to the Birkhoff-Poritsky conjecture; I did not confirm that from a primary source.
events.doubts: Whether the Treschev example would be integrable in the sense of the conjecture is not stated in the abstract I read.
events.direction: Partial regularity for a formal candidate; no verdict on the conjecture.
events.object: A formal power-series billiard (Treschev's construction) with locally linearizable dynamics near a period-two orbit. Gevrey regular for Diophantine frequency; not shown to be analytic or convergent. It is formal and local, not an explicit global table.

events.what_happened: L. Bunimovich and R. Shapiro, 'A challenger to elliptic billiards fails: String construction over convex polygons and the Birkhoff-Poritsky conjecture', arXiv:2305.03095 (v1 4 May 2023). Shows that a billiard previously proposed as a counterexample to the Birkhoff-Poritsky conjecture (a string construction over a convex polygon) is not a counterexample. v2 was submitted 3 April 2024, inside the window, and is now withdrawn by the author.
events.revisions: v2 submitted 3 Apr 2024; withdrawn by the author (per the arXiv listing). Reason and withdrawal date not given in what I read.
events.delivers: Removes one proposed candidate counterexample: the billiard claimed to be a counterexample is not one. The abstract does not state whether that billiard is integrable. Nothing positive about the conjecture.
events.remains: All of the conjecture.
events.doubts: The arXiv v2 was withdrawn; the reason is not recorded in what I read. The abstract does not say whether the challenged billiard is integrable, so 'not a counterexample' does not say whether it is a candidate for the conjecture at all. Argument not read.

withdrawn.what: v2 (submitted 3 April 2024) withdrawn by the author; the v1 content is the version with the claim above

events.direction: Negative for one candidate counterexample; leaves the conjecture as it was.
events.object: A string-construction billiard over a convex polygon, which the authors say is the core of the dynamics for tables built this way. It is claimed to be a candidate counterexample and shown not to be one. Integrability of that billiard is not stated in the abstract.

events.what_happened: L. Baracco and O. Bernardi, 'Totally integrable symplectic billiards are ellipses', arXiv:2305.19701 (31 May 2023), Advances in Mathematics 454 (2024) 109873. A symplectic-billiard analogue of Bialy's Birkhoff theorem: a strictly convex symplectic billiard table with strictly positive boundary curvature that is totally integrable is an ellipse.
events.revisions: v1 only. Published Advances in Mathematics 2024.
events.delivers: For symplectic billiards (not Birkhoff billiards), a totally integrable strictly convex table with positive curvature is an ellipse. A different model, so it settles nothing for the Birkhoff problem.
events.remains: The Birkhoff problem entirely.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published after refereeing (referee process not visible to me)

events.direction: Analogue result for symplectic billiards; positive in that model.

events.what_happened: V. Kaloshin, C. E. Koudjinan and K. Zhang, 'Birkhoff Conjecture for nearly centrally symmetric domains', arXiv:2306.12301 (v1 21 June 2023; v2 19 September 2024), Geometric and Functional Analysis 34 (2024) 1973-2007, DOI 10.1007/s00039-024-00695-6. Perturbative version of the Bialy-Mironov centrally symmetric result: a domain close to a centrally symmetric one with an integrable billiard is an ellipse.
events.delivers: A domain close enough to a centrally symmetric one with an integrable billiard is an ellipse. The paper's formulation uses 4-rational integrability and a 3-rationally integrable caustic. A perturbative, restricted class; it does not settle the non-perturbative case.
events.remains: Domains that are not close to a centrally symmetric one; the general conjecture.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published after refereeing (referee process not visible to me)

events.doubts: The Springer page redirected and the ISTA PDF was binary, so the text read is the arXiv abstract page. The journal page range and year come from search results and from PDF page labels.
events.direction: Positive for the conjecture in a restricted (perturbative, nearly centrally symmetric) class.

events.what_happened: I. Koval, 'Billiard tables with analytic Birkhoff normal form are generically Gevrey divergent', arXiv:2403.14448 (21 March 2024). Relaxes a symmetry condition in a family of billiards with analytic integrable normal forms and shows that, for a full-measure set of parameters, the Taylor series of the table diverge, with optimal Gevrey bounds. Its abstract says the original analyticity question (the Treschev example) remains open.
events.delivers: For a broader family of formal analytic normal forms, the table series generically diverge. This is local and formal, about analyticity of normal forms near a periodic orbit. It does not touch integrability of convex tables or the global conjecture.
events.remains: The conjecture; and, per the abstract, the analyticity of the original symmetric Treschev example.
events.direction: Negative for generic analyticity of a broader class of local normal forms; no verdict on the conjecture.

events.what_happened: A. E. Mironov and S. Yin, 'Integrable Birkhoff Billiards inside Cones', arXiv:2501.12843 (22 January 2025). Shows that the billiard in a convex C3 cone in R^n is integrable: the billiard always admits a degree-two first integral in the velocity components, which gives finitely many reflections on every trajectory. Presented as the first integrable billiard whose table is neither a quadric nor built from quadric pieces. Journal version: 'Birkhoff billiards inside cones', Advances in Mathematics 501 (2026) 111101, DOI 10.1016/j.aim.2026.111101 (accepted 8 June 2026, online 22 June 2026, per the Novosibirsk institute listing).
events.revisions: v1 only on arXiv. Journal version Advances in Mathematics 2026.
events.delivers: Cones in R^n (unbounded tables; the cone is over a C3 strictly convex hypersurface with nondegenerate second fundamental form) are integrable billiard tables that are not quadrics. This is a different ambient setting from the planar, bounded, strictly convex tables the bullet asks about.
events.remains: Planar bounded strictly convex tables with a smooth boundary: whether any such integrable table exists that is not an ellipse, which is the question as posed.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted after refereeing (per the Novosibirsk listing; the Elsevier page was not reached)

events.doubts: Scope: the table is an unbounded cone in R^n, not a planar bounded closed curve, so it is not a counterexample to the bullet as worded. Whether the authors' reading of it as a 'first example' is apt for the planar question is a matter for the judging pass.
events.direction: Exhibits integrable tables that are not ellipses or quadrics, in unbounded cones in R^n. It does not decide the planar bounded question, and cuts against the conjecture only if its conclusion is read beyond the planar setting.
events.object: A class rather than a single table: billiards in convex C3 cones in R^n, integrable by an explicit degree-two first integral in the velocity components. Not a planar object and not a single explicit table; the construction is by the authors' first-integral argument.

events.what_happened: S. Baranzini, V. L. Barutello, I. De Blasi and S. Terracini, 'On the Birkhoff conjecture for Kepler billiards', arXiv:2507.08446 (11 July 2025). Kepler billiards: a particle moving under an inverse-square attraction to a centre inside a strictly convex planar table. The abstract calls it a 'partial affirmative answer to a Keplerian analogue of the classical Birkhoff-Poritsky Conjecture'. Analytic integrability at high energy forces an ellipse with the centre at a focus, except possibly for one centre position.
events.delivers: For Kepler billiards at high energy, analytic integrability forces an ellipse with the centre at a focus, apart from possibly one centre location. A different model (an extra attracting force), so it is a changed version of the question.
events.remains: Billiards without the Kepler force, which is the question as posed.
events.doubts: Only the abstract and listing were read. Later papers cite this one (see later_work_cites_it).
events.direction: Analogue result in the Kepler model; positive for the analogue, silent on the planar conjecture.
events.object: Non-elliptic domains with a focal point of the second kind, forming an infinite-dimensional family, which the authors show by numerics to be chaotic (not integrable). Per the search digest of the abstract, not checked in the full text.

events.what_happened: A. Glutsyuk, 'On complex algebraic caustics in planar and projective billiards', arXiv:2509.11257 (14 September 2025), Regular and Chaotic Dynamics 31(1) (2026) 132-149, DOI 10.1134/S1560354726010016. Defines a complex caustic (a complex algebraic curve whose complex tangents reflect onto its own complex tangents) and shows that a real planar billiard has one only if its boundary is a conic. Obtained from a solution of Bolotin's polynomial integrability conjecture, jointly with Bialy and Mironov. The abstract states that the Birkhoff conjecture remains open for boundaries that are ovals of algebraic curves.
events.revisions: v1 only on arXiv. Published RCD 2026.
events.delivers: A complex-caustic characterisation: a real planar billiard has a complex algebraic caustic only if its boundary is a conic (and analogues for constant-curvature and projective billiards). This is a different notion (complex caustics), not integrability of real tables.
events.remains: The conjecture as posed. The abstract says it is open even for algebraic-oval boundaries.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published after refereeing (referee process not visible to me)

events.direction: Consistent with ellipses (conic boundaries); not a verdict on integrable tables.

events.what_happened: M. Bialy and A. E. Mironov, 'Integrable Billiards and Related Topics', arXiv:2510.03790 (submitted 4 October 2025; v2 18 October 2025). A survey covering Birkhoff, outer, magnetic, Minkowski and wire billiards and billiards in cones. Its introduction says the Birkhoff-Poritsky conjecture 'remains unsolved in full generality'; it lists the algebraic version (Glutsyuk) as completed, the local versions near ellipses, and open questions, including one on whether the boundary is an ellipse under total integrability.
events.delivers: No new result. A status statement by the field's own experts: the general conjecture is unsolved; the algebraic version is solved; local versions hold near ellipses.
events.remains: All of the conjecture as posed.

checked_by.who: M. Bialy and A. E. Mironov
checked_by.qualification: Authors of the centrally symmetric result and of the reduction used in the algebraic result
checked_by.what_they_did: Wrote a survey whose status statement says the conjecture 'remains unsolved in full generality'

events.direction: No change in the conjecture's status; reconfirms that the general case is open.

events.what_happened: P. Bishop, S. Chenoweth, E. Fleurantin, E. Sander and J. Mireles James, 'Dynamics of perturbed elliptical billiard tables', arXiv:2602.15272 (v1 17 February 2026; v2 1 October 2026). Uses the parameterization method to compute high-order Taylor expansions of local stable and unstable manifolds of periodic orbits of perturbed elliptical billiard maps, locates transverse intersections, and extends the manifolds numerically to suggest where chaotic invariant sets may exist. The paper states that the method is 'well suited for computer assisted proofs' and that a follow-up will validate the computations.
events.delivers: Numerical computation for perturbed ellipses. No rigorous theorem; the paper says rigorous validation is deferred to a follow-up. It does not claim a proof or sketch of the global conjecture.
events.remains: All of the conjecture.
events.doubts: Numerical and not rigorous. The HTML text (read in full) makes no claim about the global conjecture, and contains no 'curve shortening' material. A search digest had attributed to this paper a claimed global proof via curve shortening; I could not support that (see disputes).
events.direction: No direction on the conjecture; numerical evidence about dynamics of perturbed ellipses.

events.what_happened: K. Czudek, J. De Simoi, A. Gad and M. Poon, 'Yet another characterization of Birkhoff billiards inside discs', arXiv:2603.16468 (v1 17 March 2026; v2 18 March 2026). Main theorem: a smooth domain is a disc if and only if the first-order correction X1 in the Lazutkin coordinates vanishes. No integrability hypothesis is assumed. Integrability enters only in a remark citing Bialy's circle theorem.
events.delivers: Characterises discs (the circle special case of the conjecture) by the vanishing of a Lazutkin invariant, with no integrability assumption. It says nothing about ellipses other than discs.
events.remains: All ellipses that are not circles; and the integrable hypothesis as posed.
events.direction: Circle special case; neither cuts for nor against the conjecture's ellipse conclusion beyond discs.

events.what_happened: A. E. Mironov and S. Yin, 'Integrability of Billiards Inside Cones as a Discrete-Time Hamiltonian System', arXiv:2603.28347 (30 March 2026). Follow-up to the 2025 cones paper: the cone billiard has n-1 independent commuting first integrals and is completely integrable as a discrete-time Hamiltonian system.
events.delivers: For the same class of cone billiards, complete integrability as a discrete-time Hamiltonian system. Cones only.
events.remains: Planar bounded strictly convex tables.
events.doubts: Scope is cones, not planar tables; the same caveat as the 2025 paper applies.
events.direction: Same as the 2025 cones paper: integrable non-quadric tables in cones, outside the planar bounded setting.
events.object: The same class of cone billiards as the 2025 paper; integrability via n-1 commuting first integrals.

events.what_happened: L. Liu and P. A. S. Salomao, 'Birkhoff conjecture and finite energy foliations in Hill's lunar problem', arXiv:2606.12912 (11 June 2026). A namesake: Birkhoff's retrograde-orbit conjecture for Hill's lunar problem in celestial mechanics. The abstract says it proves the conjecture for energies below critical (a disc-like global surface of section bounded by the retrograde orbit) and builds finite energy foliations above critical. Not billiards.
events.delivers: Birkhoff's retrograde-orbit conjecture for Hill's lunar problem below the critical energy, and finite energy foliations above it. A different question sharing a namesake.
events.remains: Not applicable: a different problem. Nothing here about integrable billiards.
events.direction: Not about the billiard problem.

events.what_happened: S. Baranzini and S. Terracini, 'Analytic rigidity and symbolic dynamics for two-centre billiards', arXiv:2609.02310 (2 September 2026). For planar two-centre billiards, a dichotomy: integrable at every energy (expected only for confocal ellipses) or chaotic. With real-analytic boundary, invariant real-analytic functions are constant; the abstract calls this the real-analytic form of a 'two-centre Birkhoff-Poritsky conjecture'.
events.delivers: Analogue for two-centre (Kepler-type) billiards: a sharp dichotomy and analytic rigidity. It is not the planar Birkhoff problem.
events.remains: The planar Birkhoff problem as posed.
events.direction: Analogue in a two-centre model; silent on the planar conjecture.

events.what_happened: Z. Lai, L.-H. Lim and J. Ren, 'Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture is false', arXiv:2609.10420 (9 September 2026). A namesake: the Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture in real algebraic geometry (piecewise-quadratic functions as lattice combinations of polynomials). The abstract says the counterexample was found with the assistance of a multi-agent, multi-model setup, and the search digest names GPT 5.6, GPT 6, Claude Opus 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 in that setup. This is not the billiard problem and the models are credited for that other problem only.
events.delivers: Not about this problem. Claimed counterexample to the Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture; not checked by me.
events.remains: Not applicable.
events.doubts: The AI involvement and the model names are stated only in the abstract text I read and a search snippet. They do not bear on the billiard problem. I did not verify the counterexample or the model names.
events.direction: Not about the billiard problem.

disputes.summary: The conjecture is usually called Birkhoff's (or Birkhoff-Poritsky). Secondary sources say Birkhoff posed it, and Poritsky first printed it in 1950 with the attribution to Birkhoff. The naming is conventional, not a dispute about credit.

A search digest said arXiv:2602.15272 (Bishop et al., February 2026) sketches a proof of the complete global Birkhoff conjecture via a novel curve shortening flow. I read the abstract page, the full HTML and its reference list: the paper claims no such proof or sketch, and 'curve shortening' does not appear in its text. The only curve shortening material I found is the affine length-shortening strategy outlined in Kaloshin and Sorrentino (arXiv:1612.09194, Appendix F; introduction read, appendix not extractable). That is presented as a plan, not an argument.
The Glutsyuk polynomial-integrability result is described as requiring a connected C2 boundary in a search digest, but the arXiv abstract I read says 'smooth'. The JEMS text was not read.
Bialy's theorem on totally integrable billiards is dated 1993 in one secondary source and 1992 in another (Baracco and Bernardi). The paper itself was not read.
Bunimovich and Shapiro (arXiv:2305.03095): v2, submitted 3 April 2024, is withdrawn by the author. The reason is not given in what I read.

summary: No event since 26 January 2024 settles the planar conjecture as worded, and every in-window paper I read either states it is open or does something narrower. The restricted results that bear on it are older. Poritsky (1950) printed the statement and gave a partial result under a nested-caustic assumption (secondary report only). Bialy (1993) proved the circle case under global total integrability (secondary report only). Kaloshin and Sorrentino (arXiv December 2012 on conjugacy, which reformulates the conjecture; arXiv December 2016 on the local version, Annals 2018), Avila, De Simoi and Kaloshin (arXiv December 2014; Annals 2016), and Huang, Kaloshin and Sorrentino (arXiv May 2017; GAFA 2018) prove local versions near ellipses. Glutsyuk (arXiv June 2017; JEMS 2021) proves the polynomially integrable version. Bialy and Mironov (arXiv August 2020; Annals 2022) prove the centrally symmetric C2 case under foliation or first-integral hypotheses. Koval (arXiv November 2021) proves the almost-every-ellipse local case, and Huang (Acta 2022) integrability-away-from-the-boundary. Kaloshin, Koudjinan and Zhang (arXiv June 2023; GAFA 2024) prove the perturbative version of the centrally symmetric case. Wang and Zhang (arXiv November 2022) show Treschev's formal local example is Gevrey but not known to converge. Bunimovich and Shapiro (arXiv May 2023) show one candidate counterexample is not one; v2 was withdrawn in April 2024. Baracco and Bernardi (arXiv May 2023; Advances 2024) prove the symplectic-billiard analogue. In the window: Koval's March 2024 Gevrey result concerns formal local normal forms, not integrability; Mironov and Yin (arXiv January 2025; Advances in Mathematics 2026) show billiards in convex C3 cones in R^n are integrable and not quadrics, which is the closest thing to a non-elliptic integrable table, but the table is unbounded and non-planar, so its bearing on the planar question is for the judging pass; Baranzini et al. (July 2025), Baranzini and Terracini (September 2026) are Kepler and two-centre analogues; Glutsyuk (September 2025) classifies complex caustics for real planar billiards and says the Birkhoff conjecture is open even for algebraic-oval boundaries; Bialy and Mironov (October 2025) say the conjecture 'remains unsolved in full generality'; Czudek et al. (March 2026) characterise discs by a Lazutkin invariant without an integrability hypothesis; Bishop et al. (February 2026) is numerical, with rigorous validation deferred. Koval gave a talk on the 2021 local result at Beijing Normal University on 12 May 2026, which is not a new event. Two namesakes are recorded and discarded: Liu and Salomao (June 2026) on Birkhoff's retrograde-orbit conjecture for Hill's lunar problem, and Lai, Lim and Ren (September 2026) on the Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture, the last of which credits GPT and Claude models for a different problem. Nothing in the record names an AI system as contributing to the billiard mathematics; I searched for lab announcements, AI trackers, Lean formalisations and AI-named billiard papers and found none. The Wikipedia article for this conjecture could not be located (two guessed titles returned 404; the Dynamical billiards article states the elliptic case only). Close calls: (i) whether the 2025-2026 cone results should count as movement on this problem, since they show non-quadric integrable tables but not planar ones; (ii) whether the restricted local and centrally-symmetric results (which are old, so outside the window) should count as partial resolutions of the problem as worded.
competing_reading: The cone results (Mironov and Yin, 2025 and 2026) are the strongest case that something moved in the window: they exhibit integrable billiard tables that are neither ellipses nor quadrics, which is what the conjecture's conclusion would have to rule out if the planar hypothesis were relaxed. A reader who treats the planar bounded setting as incidental would count this as a counterexample-type event. The strongest case against that reading is the scope: the tables are unbounded cones in R^n, the authors do not claim a planar counterexample, and the problem as worded asks about planar, strictly convex, closed tables. A second reading treats the restricted results as partial resolutions of the problem as worded (for example, Bialy and Mironov's centrally symmetric theorem with its foliation hypotheses). The case against that reading is that each one changes the hypothesis (centrally symmetric, nearly centrally symmetric, small eccentricity, polynomial integrals, integrability near the boundary, or Kepler force), so none settles the problem as the bullet states it.
what_would_settle_it: (a) The intended notion of integrability and the smoothness class, from the bullet's wording and the list's own definition. Without these, a 'resolution' is not well defined. (b) A primary-source check of whether any cone result yields a bounded, planar, strictly convex, smooth table that is integrable and not an ellipse. (c) Reading Appendix F of arXiv:1612.09194 and the published Acta and GAFA texts, to confirm the exact hypotheses of the local results. (d) The full text of Mironov and Yin (2025), to check whether their 'first example' is asserted for planar tables or only for cones. (e) Referee or expert commentary on the Koval 2021 preprint, which I could not find, and on the Czudek et al. and Bishop et al. preprints. (f) A proof of convergence for the Treschev example, or a non-convergence result, which would bear on the local version.
